$comment: The recorded MINIMUM size of each suite, as `assert_known_failures.py`
measures it from the JUnit report the run produced.
-- What this is for, argued from the workflow rather than from an incident -
A suite that does not run can report success, and this is provable by
READING `.github/workflows/checks.yml` and `assert_known_failures.py`. It
does not depend on reproducing any particular incident, and the argument is
put this way deliberately: a guard justified only by an anecdote gets deleted
by the next person who cannot reproduce the anecdote.
Three facts, each checkable in the files themselves:
1. Both suite steps run under `set +e` and abort only when the status
EXCEEDS 1. Exit 1 is the tolerated path by design -- the frontend suite
legitimately exits 1 on its two allowlisted failures. So a truncated run
that exits 1 passes that step.
2. `assert_known_failures.py`'s allowlist rules reason only about failures
IN the report: an unlisted failure, a listed test that passed, a listed
test that is absent. A report cannot fail a test it does not contain.
3. Therefore the only thing that could notice a short run was rule (2)'s
last clause -- an ALLOWLISTED test going missing -- which is an accident
of which files were lost. Drop any set of files containing no allowlisted
test and the job exits 0 having run a fraction of the suite. On the
backend that accident is not even available in principle: a suite whose
allowlist is empty has no named test whose absence could be noticed.
Nothing anywhere measured how big the suite should be. This file is that
measurement, and it closes (3) by not depending on which files were lost.
The observation that prompted the work is consistent with the above and is
recorded as an observation, not as the load-bearing argument: under memory
pressure `npm test` reported `Test Files  40 passed (40)` while 21 of 61
files never started -- not '21 failed'; vitest believed there were forty. It
has resisted repetition on some machines and reproduced readily on others.
The hole above is there either way.
Adding tests NEVER fails this check. A recorded expected total would be
wrong within a day and would train people to edit the number without reading
it -- which is how `known_test_failures.json` would have rotted had it not
been built to self-prune. Only a run that comes back SMALLER fails.
There is no slack, and that is a deliberate difference from
`frontend/bundle-budget.json`. The bundle ratchet allows 0.5% drift because
gzip output is not byte-identical across zlib versions -- it is absorbing
instrument noise. These are integer counts; there is no instrument and no
noise. Any allowance here would not absorb error, it would be a hole of
exactly that size for tests to disappear into: 5% of the frontend suite is
43 tests that could vanish in silence.
(Collection is platform-stable in this repository, which is what makes that
affordable. Every `skipif` in `backend/tests` is a RUNTIME skip, so a skipped
test is still collected and still writes a `<testcase>`; there is no
`collect_ignore` anywhere. The numbers below were measured on Windows and
are enforced on ubuntu-latest, and it is the absence of collection-time
platform gates that makes that sound rather than lucky.)
Same reasoning as the bundle budget's SHRINK_ALLOWANCE: a baseline that can
only ever move one way rots. A floor that is never re-staked decays into a
floor at zero -- record 5,251 today, let the backend suite reach 12,000 over
a year, and a run executing 6,000 tests sails through while having lost half
the suite. So a run more than 25% above a recorded floor fails too, and
prints the number to write. That is loose on purpose: it is not absorbing
measurement error, it is choosing how often a human is asked to look, and a
quarter of a suite is rare enough to be a real event.
Deleting tests is legitimate. Deleting them BY ACCIDENT is what this file
catches, and the difference is that the first arrives as a diff somebody
reviewed. So lower the number in the SAME COMMIT that removes the tests, and
say in the message what was removed. The check prints the exact number.
If you are lowering it because CI told you to and you did not remove any
tests, do not lower it -- that is the infrastructure failure this exists to
surface, and the run should be repeated instead.
cases -- a count of `<testcase>` ELEMENTS in the report. Elements, not
distinct `classname::name` ids: a real frontend report measured while this
was written held 585 elements collapsing to 577 ids, so against ids one of
a duplicated pair could stop running without moving the number.
files -- distinct `classname` values. For vitest that is the test file's
path, so one classname is one file. For pytest it is the dotted module path
with the test class appended where there is one, so a module holding two
`Test*` classes contributes three. It is not literally a file count on the
backend and the check does not claim it is; it is stable run to run, and it
is the number that moves first and hardest when a worker dies, because a
dead worker takes whole files with it.
backend  -- `python -m pytest tests --junitxml=junit-backend.xml`, the
default run (`live_infra` and `browser` deselected by pyproject.toml).
Reported `1 failed, 5240 passed, 10 skipped, 514 deselected`, the single
failure being the allowlisted one.
frontend -- `npm test -- --reporter=junit`, the repository's own `test`
script, which exits non-zero on a correct run because of the two
allowlisted failures in `src/domains/registry.test.ts`.
